unit4.q: A sample of 50 batches of acid solution had a mean pH of 2.6 with population standard deviation 0.3. To test H₀: μ ≤ 2.5 versus H₁: μ > 2.5, the P-value is:
unit4.note: No listed option is correct for the stated data: z = 2.3570 and one-sided P ≈ 0.00921. A (0.0087) is the nearest listed option, but is not the calculated answer.

unit4.q: A sample of 50 copper wires had a mean resistance of 1.03 mΩ with a standard deviation of 0.1 mΩ. Let μ represent the mean resistance of copper wires of this type. The null and alternative hypotheses for testing whether the mean resistance is greater than 1 mΩ are:
A sample of 65 electric motors had a mean efficiency of 0.595 with a standard deviation of 0.05. To test H₀: μ ≥ 0.6 versus H₁: μ < 0.6, the test statistic is:
unit4.note: A is the intended large-sample z-test answer in this section. Since the standard deviation is estimated, an exact normal-population t-test would use C with 64 df; both have the same numeric statistic.

unit4.q: A process manufactures ball bearings with diameters normally distributed with mean 2.505 cm and standard deviation 0.008 cm. A sample of 100 bearings has a mean diameter of 2.507 cm. To test H₀: μ = 2.505 versus H₁: μ ≠ 2.505, the P-value is:
unit4.note: z = 2.5, so two-sided P ≈ 0.01242. The portal concatenated all four options into option A; separated here.

unit4.q: A chemical process produces yields with population standard deviation 5. A sample of 50 runs has a mean yield of 82. To test H₀: μ ≤ 80 versus H₁: μ > 80 at α = 0.05, the conclusion is:
options: Do not reject H₀ because z = 2.83 < 1.96
Do not reject H₀ because the P-value is 0.0023
unit4.note: A uses the correct one-sided 5% critical value. C states a true inequality and reaches the same decision, but 1.96 is not the appropriate one-sided 5% cutoff.

unit4.q: A hypothesis test has P = 0.04. At the 1% level of significance, the conclusion is:
A hypothesis test produces a P-value of 0.22. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?
options: There is strong evidence against H₀
H₀ is plausible; we fail to reject it
unit4.note: At conventional significance levels, such as 5% or 10%.

unit4.q: A test has P = 0.03. Which statement is correct?
options: H₀ is rejected at the 1% level
H₀ is not rejected at the 5% level
H₀ is rejected at the 5% level but not at the 1% level
H₀ is rejected at both the 5% and 1% levels

unit4.q: If a hypothesis test results in “failing to reject H₀”, which of the following is the correct interpretation?
options: H₀ is plausible, but not proven true
The sample size was too small

unit4.q: A 99% confidence interval for μ is (5.1,5.8). To test H₀: μ = 6 versus H₁: μ ≠ 6, the P-value will be:
options: Cannot be determined from the interval alone

unit4.q: A 95% confidence interval for μ is (94.6,98.3). A researcher tests H₀: μ = 100 versus H₁: μ ≠ 100 and obtains a P-value of 0.12. Which is correct?
options: The confidence interval and hypothesis test contradict each other
The P-value should be less than 0.05
unit4.note: Both B and C are correct if the CI and test use the same method and data. The CI excludes 100, so the corresponding two-sided P must be below 0.05. The information does not identify which reported result was calculated incorrectly.

options: H₀ is not rejected at the 0.05 level

options: Reject H₀ because 30 is in the interval
Fail to reject H₀ because 30 is in the interval
Reject H₀ because the interval is narrow

options: Reject H₀ because 50 is in the interval

unit4.note: The portal randomizes question order, so “previous mcq” can appear before the data. Using n = 6, x̄ = 39.011, s = 0.0119 and μ₀ = 39 gives t ≈ 2.2643, df = 5 and P ≈ 0.073.

unit4.note: No option is numerically correct: t = (39.011 − 39)/(0.0119/√6) ≈ 2.2643 with 5 df. A is the likely intended option because its distribution and df are correct.

options: Student’s t distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
unit4.note: For the standard one-sample test with unknown population variance and approximately normal population.

unit4.q: In a one-way ANOVA, the total variation in the data is partitioned into which two components?
options: Type I variation and Type II variation
Explained variation and residual variation only
unit4.note: C can also describe the same decomposition when “explained” means between-group and “residual” means within-group. A is the standard ANOVA terminology and intended answer.

unit4.q: Three different machines are compared for mean tensile strength. Five wires are sampled per machine. ANOVA table: Between SS = 120, df = 2, MS = 60; Within SS = 240, df = 12, MS = 20; Total SS = 360, df = 14. What is F?
unit4.note: F = MS_between/MS_within = 60/20 = 3.

unit4.note: Expected counts = 20,140,30,10; χ² = 2.13333.

unit4.note: The listed observed counts sum to 572, not 600. B follows the stated sample size of 600; if the listed counts are the complete data, expected counts would be 572/6 ≈ 95.333, which is not offered.

unit4.note: Assuming no distribution parameters were estimated from the sample.

unit4.note: Using the printed margins, E = 200×66/500 = 26.4. The source table is inconsistent: Machine 1 cells sum to 130, Machine 2 to 201, and the Too Thick column sums to 33. Using only the body cells gives n = 511 and E ≈ 25.961, not an offered answer.

options: Reject H₀; the loci are not in linkage equilibrium
Do not reject H₀; there is no evidence that the loci are not in linkage equilibrium
Reject H₀; the loci are in linkage equilibrium
Do not reject H₀; the loci are definitely in linkage equilibrium

unit4.note: No listed option is correct: E = row total×column total/grand total = 37×27/74 = 13.5.

unit4.q: The article “Inconsistent Health Perceptions for US Women and Men with Diabetes” presents income by gender. Printed headers: Poor, Near Poor, Low Middle, High. Printed male entries: 156,77,25,35,13604. Female entries: 348,152,43,35,92511. The chi-square statistic for independence is:
unit4.note: The source table is malformed: 4 income headers but 5 numeric entries per row. No defensible option can be selected without corrected data. Treating all 5 printed values as separate category counts gives χ² ≈ 351.70, which is not offered.

unit4.q: At an assembly plant, weld quality by shift (High,Moderate,Low) is: Day = 467,191,42; Evening = 445,171,34; Night = 254,129,17. What is the expected frequency for Day—High quality?
unit4.note: No listed option is correct. Day total = 700, High total = 1166, grand total = 1750; expected = 700×1166/1750 = 466.4.

unit4.q: A Type II error is made when:

H₀ is not rejected at the 1% level

H₀ is true and we reject it

Concluding the process is calibrated when it is actually out of calibration

Concluding the process is calibrated when it is actually out of calibration

unit4.note: More precisely, failing to detect that the process is out of calibration. The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.

unit4.q: A test is conducted at the 5% level with H₀: μ = 100 versus H₁: μ > 100. Population standard deviation σ = 15 and n = 36. The rejection region is:
unit4.note: No listed option is correct: x̄ > 100 + 1.64485×15/√36 ≈ 104.112. The 104.9 option would approximately match a two-sided 5% cutoff, not the stated one-sided test.

unit4.q: A fixed-level test is conducted at the 10% significance level. The rejection region consists of:
options: The middle 90% of the null distribution
The most extreme 10% of the null distribution (one or both tails depending on H₁)
The most extreme 5% of the null distribution
unit4.note: The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.

unit4.q: In a fixed-level test, if the significance level is α = 0.05 and the P-value is 0.03, the correct decision is:
options: Do not reject H₀ because P > α
Do not reject H₀ because P ≤ α
unit4.note: The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.

unit4.note: For the same test design, variability and fixed alternative effect.

options: Use a two-tailed test instead of a one-tailed test
unit4.note: The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.

unit4.q: The power of a test is defined as:
options: The probability of a Type I error
The probability of a Type II error
The probability of rejecting H₀ when it is false
The probability of failing to reject H₀ when it is true
unit4.note: The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.

unit4.q: If the significance level α is increased (e.g., from 0.01 to 0.05), the power of the test will:
unit4.note: Holding sample size, test design, variability and alternative effect fixed.

unit4.q: A test has power 0.90 when μ = 15. This means:
options: The probability of rejecting H₀ when μ = 15 is 0.90

The probability of failing to reject H₀ when μ = 15 is 0.90

unit4.q: A test has power 0.80 when μ = 8 and power 0.95 when μ = 10. This indicates that:
options: The test is better at detecting a larger departure from H₀
The test is better at detecting a smaller departure from H₀
The power does not depend on the alternative value of μ

unit4.note: Intended answer assumes μ = 10 is farther from the null mean than μ = 8. The null mean is omitted from the question.

unit4.q: A test has a Type I error probability of 0.05 and a Type II error probability of 0.20. The power of the test is:
For a fixed sample size and significance level, power is highest when:
options: The alternative mean is close to the null mean
The alternative mean is far from the null mean
The population standard deviation is large
The test is two-tailed rather than one-tailed

unit4.q: If the significance level α is decreased from 0.05 to 0.01, the power of the test will:
unit4.note: Holding other factors fixed.

unit4.q: A one-tailed test and a two-tailed test use the same data with α = 0.05. The one-tailed test has:
options: Lower power than the two-tailed test
Higher power than the two-tailed test (when the effect is in the specified direction)

unit4.q: A researcher wants to reduce both Type I and Type II error probabilities simultaneously. The most effective approach is to:
options: Increase α and decrease the sample size
Decrease α and increase the sample size
Increase both α and the sample size
Decrease both α and the sample size
unit4.note: Increase the sample size enough to offset the loss in power from lowering α. The source concatenated all options into A; separated here.
